tagline: A desert road follows the Salt River toward Roosevelt Dam.
intro: The Apache Trail corridor takes SR 88 from Apache Junction through desert terrain toward Roosevelt Dam. Two lanes lead into Tonto National Forest and along Canyon Lake’s southern shore; beyond Tortilla Flat, an unpaved section winds through the Superstition Mountains. Wikipedia identifies part of SR 88 as the state-designated Apache Trail Historic Road and the eastern corridor as a National Forest Scenic Byway.

At Tortilla Flat, road building and dam building were linked: the settlement served freight haulers heading to Roosevelt Dam’s construction site in 1904. Tourists and mail carriers later used its stage stop through the 1930s. The route received the number 88 in 1927; paving reached the Apache Junction-to-Canyon Lake section in the late 1940s. In 2019, the Woodbury Fire and subsequent flooding damaged the unpaved road, closing the section between mileposts 222 and 229.

From Apache Junction, the road passes Goldfield before entering the national forest and reaching Canyon Lake. After Tortilla Flat, the corridor winds east, approaches Apache Lake and follows the Salt River northeast to Roosevelt Dam. The highway once continued toward Globe, but that eastern extension became SR 188 in 1999. Pavement returns near the dam, and SR 88 meets SR 188 beside Roosevelt Lake.

moments.title: Canyon Lake
moments.text: Canyon Lake is the smallest of four reservoirs created along the Salt River as part of the Salt River Project. Mormon Flat Dam formed it after two years of construction, completed in 1925. The lake covers 950 acres, with Apache Lake and Roosevelt Lake upstream and Saguaro Lake downstream. SR 88 follows part of its southern shore before turning away from the river toward Tortilla Flat. Its place on the route puts Canyon Lake before Tortilla Flat, Apache Lake and Roosevelt Lake. The Forest Service manages recreation amenities here, including hiking trails, camping and boating.
moments.notice: The road follows part of Canyon Lake’s southern shore.

moments.title: Tortilla Flat
moments.text: Tortilla Flat’s stagecoach past survives in the place, but many of its buildings are replacements. Wikipedia calls it the last surviving stagecoach stop along the Apache Trail. Before the freight camp, prospectors searching the Superstition Mountains used Tortilla Flat as a camping ground. A freight camp for Roosevelt Dam construction, it later served tourists and mail carriers through the 1930s. Flooding in 1942 damaged the settlement and prompted many residents to leave. Fire later destroyed the store, restaurant and motel; most of the present commercial buildings date from rebuilding in the late 1980s.

moments.title: Theodore Roosevelt Dam
moments.text: Roosevelt Dam’s concrete exterior encloses an older masonry structure. Completed in 1911, the original dam stood 280 feet high; the expansion begun in 1989 raised it to 357 feet. The work finished in 1996 and included rerouting Highway 188 over a new bridge upstream. That transformation changed its historical status as well as its appearance: the National Historic Landmark designation was withdrawn in 1999 after reconstruction altered its original design and materials. Its main functions are irrigation, water supply and flood control, with hydroelectric generation as well. The dam impounds the Salt River to form Roosevelt Lake.
moments.notice: The concrete exterior covers the original rubble-masonry dam.

practical: Tortilla Flat: Wikipedia reports a high-clearance four-wheel-drive and utility-terrain-vehicle restriction following SR 88’s September 2024 reopening. (checked 2026-10-11)
